It is indeed unfortunate that many countries are reporting "death with SARS-CoV-2" as the same as "death by SARS-CoV-2." especially since the US at at least goes to such great lengths to separate other causes out of influenza deaths.

Unfortunately, it isn't known at this time whether every piece of data was or was not affected by this overreporting, nor which places are doing it. We know some - Italy, e.g. - but it would be just as incorrect to adjust some data but not others based on incomplete knowledge of what needed adjusting, than to use unadjusted data that was known to be incorrect.

Until an after-the-fact analysis can be carried out once the whole thing has run its course, the best us laypeople will be able to do is look for an increase in total mortality in a region. If/when you see a a statistically significant spike in total mortality, you can conclude that there is some other source of death that is more than all the other typical sources of death. You still won't be able to prove it from that alone, but the prime suspect for that would be SARS-CoV-2, if cases were still rolling in when that spike manifested.

For example, if your region typically experiences 100 deaths per month, and they claim that there are 50 SARS-CoV-2 deaths per month, and this month your region reports 102 deaths... it is entirely possible that all of those SARS-CoV-2 deaths were people that died of other causes while simply having the virus, rather than people that died of the virus.

But if the next month your region reports 200 deaths, instead of the typical monthly 100, now you know that something is going on and that at least 100 deaths are from some atypical nonstandard source.

That is a more sound, but very late indicator.
